summary:
Section 33 of Canada’s Charter—the notwithstanding clause—allows federal, provincial, and territorial legislatures to make a law operate despite certain Charter rights. A law must expressly identify the rights being overridden; the clause cannot be invoked implicitly and requires only the ordinary legislative process and a simple majority.

The clause applies to fundamental freedoms (section 2), legal rights (sections 7–14), and equality rights (section 15). It does not override democratic, mobility, language, or other rights outside those provisions. A declaration lasts no more than five years, though a legislature can renew it. The time limit is intended to make elected officials answerable to voters. Invoking the clause blocks courts from assessing the law against the rights specifically overridden, but does not remove every possible legal or constitutional challenge.

The clause was a compromise in the 1981 negotiations that led to the Charter. Provinces worried that the Charter would shift too much power from elected legislatures to the courts. Its inclusion helped secure agreement on the constitutional package, though Quebec’s government did not endorse the deal. The clause is often described as balancing written rights and judicial review with Canada’s tradition of parliamentary supremacy.

Use has been concentrated in Quebec, which applied the clause broadly to its laws from 1982 to 1985 and later used it for measures involving French-language signs, religious symbols worn by certain public employees, and the use of French. Other examples include Saskatchewan’s 1986 strike-breaking law; Ontario’s 2021 election-advertising restrictions and 2022 law restricting education workers’ strike rights; and Alberta’s 2025 back-to-work legislation for teachers. Alberta also used the clause in a 2000 law defining marriage as between a man and a woman, but the article says that law exceeded provincial authority. Several proposed uses were abandoned, including New Brunswick’s proposed vaccination measure and Ontario’s proposed response to a court ruling on Toronto’s electoral wards. The federal government has never invoked the clause.

The article also notes that similar override mechanisms exist in some Canadian rights laws and in other jurisdictions, though their scope differs. It presents the clause as a distinctive Canadian device for balancing legislative authority against constitutional rights and the courts.
